Well, I don't know the exact number this morning, but my regular doctor is the one who sent me here because my weight has dropped so low. He and everyone else are just making this huge fuss about it, saying I'm way below what's normal for someone my height. But I honestly feel like being this light helps me keep up with the shop. I wouldn't say I judge myself on how I look. I mean, my body is just the thing that gets me through the day, you know? If I'm judging myself on anything, it's my craftsmanship.

So, yeah, craftsmanship and respect for the trade, that's what's important to me. Not really... what did you say? Body shape? No, I don't really think about that as who I am.

Well, I wouldn't call it an intense fear, but... yeah, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have those foods we used to make for the holidays, I do start worrying right away. I just think I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep.

It was a nightmare to calibrate, the thermostat was always off by at least twenty degrees, so you had to keep an oven thermometer in there and constantly adjust the dial. I actually tried to fix the door hinge on it once when I was in my twenties, but the springs were so rusted I ended up having to fabricate a custom bracket in my buddy's metal shop just to get it to close flush. 

Anyway, my brother always wanted to carve the roast, but he’d use this dull carving knife that he refused to sharpen. He’d just hack at the meat instead of slicing it against the grain. It drove me absolutely crazy. A dull blade is more dangerous than a sharp one, I always tell Mark that. You end up putting too much force behind it, and that’s when it slips and you end up in the ER getting stitches on Christmas Eve. Which actually happened to my uncle Pete back in '98, sliced right through his thumb... 

But yeah, I just... I worry about losing control and gaining weight if I eat those kinds of things. It's just easier to stick to what I know works.

Perfect? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I like things done right, sure, but I don't obsess over it being flawless outside of work. I just do what needs to be done. 

Speaking of getting things done, I finally got around to fixing the latch on the back gate yesterday. It's been driving me up the wall for weeks. The frost heave over the winter completely threw the alignment off. You know how it is with wooden fences, the ground freezes and thaws, and the posts shift. It's a classic problem with pressure-treated pine if you don't set the posts deep enough below the frost line. Whoever put that fence in—probably the previous owner—didn't dig the holes anywhere near the forty-two inches they should have been. They probably just used a post-hole digger, hit a rock at two feet, and called it a day. 

So the gate was sagging, and the latch wouldn't catch unless you lifted the whole door up by the handle. I had to take the whole mechanism off, plug the old screw holes with dowels and wood glue, and let it cure overnight. You can't just drive new screws into stripped wood, it'll hold for maybe a week before it pulls out again. I ended up having to shim the hinges with some thin brass plate I had lying around just to get the gap even. Brass is great for that, it won't rust like steel when it's exposed to the weather. 

Anyway, it closes with a nice, satisfying click now. But yeah, perfectionism? Not really. I just like things to work the way they're supposed to.

No, I... I don't feel like that. I don't walk around feeling heavy at all. 

Speaking of heavy, though, you want to know what really makes you feel heavy? A fully loaded leather tool belt. When I first started out, I bought this gorgeous Occidental Leather rig. Though, honestly, even then, it just moves the pain from your lumbar spine right up to your trapezius muscles. It's an ergonomic nightmare. I finally gave up and switched to a ballistic nylon rig about five years ago. Best decision I ever made. 

The nylon doesn't hold up quite as well to abrasion, of course. Well, it's not about what they think, it's... I mean, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have, you know, the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays, I just start worrying right away. I worry that I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep.

I was restoring this antique drawknife last weekend—beautiful piece of high-carbon steel, probably from the late eighteen-hundreds, back when they really knew how to forge a blade. The edge retention on those old tools is incredible. You can get them sharp enough to shave with if you spend enough time on a leather strop with some green honing compound. 

But the handles! They were completely loose. The wood had shrunk over the last century, and the tangs were just rattling around inside. People think you can just soak them in linseed oil to swell the wood back up, but that's a myth. It just makes a sticky mess and doesn't fix the structural integrity. You actually have to pull the handles off, wrap the tangs in a layer of thin brass shim stock—there's that brass again, see, it's so useful—and then drive them back in with a wooden mallet. You have to use a wooden mallet, or a dead-blow hammer, because if you hit the end of the handle with a steel hammer, you'll split the hickory right down the grain. 

Anyway, I spent three hours just getting those handles seated properly. It takes a lot of control to get it right without ruining the antique wood. But yeah... what were you asking? Oh, gaining weight. Yeah, if I eat those heavy foods, I just feel like I'm losing control of everything.

It takes hours to get the backs perfectly flat. \n\nMy apprentice, Mark—he's twenty-two, nice enough kid, but completely clueless sometimes—he actually tried to use one of those good chisels to pry open a can of wood stain last week. Not really... what did you say? Body shape? No, I don't really think about that as who I am.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel that even though you're underweight, you still have areas of your body where you feel you carry too much fat or aren't lean enough?\n\nPatient: I mean... no, I don't really think so. The mechanic there, Luis, he's been working on it since I bought it. He told me the transmission is starting to slip and it's going to cost a fortune to rebuild. I was just sitting in his waiting room, drinking this terrible stale coffee from a styrofoam cup, looking at all these faded posters of spark plugs on the wall, thinking about how I'm going to pay for it. It's a classic problem with pressure-treated pine if you don't set the posts deep enough below the frost line. Whoever put that fence in—probably the previous owner—didn't dig the holes anywhere near the forty-two inches they should have been. It's like lifting solid concrete. It's got to be pushing forty-seven pounds per cubic foot. Wait, didn't we just cover this? I feel like you just asked me about feeling heavy. And like I said before, no. I don't feel heavier than I am. I really don't.

Anxious? No, I wouldn't say I get anxious for no reason. I mean, if I'm worried about something, there's usually a pretty good reason for it. I'm a pretty practical person. 

Speaking of practical, I was just thinking about how impractical most modern hardware is. You go to the big box store to buy hinges for a cabinet door, and everything is that cheap pot metal from overseas. It looks shiny in the package, but the minute you put any real torque on the screws, the heads just snap right off. Pop! I actually had to invest in a specialized set of hollow-core extractor bits just for that. They're like these tiny little hole saws that drill around the broken screw. But even then, you have to plug the hole with a hardwood dowel, wait for the glue to cure, cut it flush with a Japanese pull saw—those saws are amazing, by the way, they cut on the pull stroke so the blade can be incredibly thin, which means less kerf and a way cleaner cut. Anyway, you have to do all that just to drill a new pilot hole and try again. It's a massive waste of time. I finally just started ordering all my hardware from this specialty supplier out of Pennsylvania. It costs three times as much, but they use actual solid brass and hardened steel. When you're hanging a solid core door that weighs eighty pounds, you can't trust cheap hinges. You just can't. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't just sit around worrying about nothing. If I'm worried, it's about something real, like a stripped screw or a deadline.

I had this job last month, doing a master bath remodel for this couple over in the new subdivision. They wanted this massive, frameless mirror covering the entire double vanity wall. It must have weighed a hundred pounds. You can't just use standard drywall anchors for something like that, you have to find the studs and use heavy-duty J-channels. And of course, the framing in that house was atrocious. The studs were supposed to be sixteen inches on center, but whoever framed that wall must have been drunk because they were completely random. I had to rip out a section of the drywall just to add horizontal blocking so I'd have something solid to screw into. \n\nAnd the dust! Drywall dust gets into absolutely everything. It's like baby powder. You have to seal off the vents, put up plastic sheeting with those zipper doors... and even then, you'll be sweeping it up for weeks. I have this industrial Shop-Vac, a real beast, 6.5 peak horsepower, but even that struggles with the fine dust unless you use the special HEPA bags. They cost a fortune, like thirty bucks for a pack of two, but if you don't use them, the dust just blows right out the exhaust port and back into the room. \n\nAnyway, what was I saying? Oh, mirrors. Yeah, I don't really spend time looking at myself. I just don't see the point.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel that anything you do is not quite good enough unless it’s absolutely perfect, even in areas of life outside of work?\n\nPatient: Perfect? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I like things done right, sure, but I don't obsess over it being flawless outside of work. I just do what needs to be done. \n\nSpeaking of getting things done, I finally got around to fixing the latch on the back gate yesterday. It's been driving me up the wall for weeks. The frost heave over the winter completely threw the alignment off. You know how it is with wooden fences, the ground freezes and thaws, and the posts shift. It's a classic problem with pressure-treated pine if you don't set the posts deep enough below the frost line. Whoever put that fence in—probably the previous owner—didn't dig the holes anywhere near the forty-two inches they should have been. They probably just used a post-hole digger, hit a rock at two feet, and called it a day. \n\nSo the gate was sagging, and the latch wouldn't catch unless you lifted the whole door up by the handle. I had to take the whole mechanism off, plug the old screw holes with dowels and wood glue, and let it cure overnight. You can't just drive new screws into stripped wood, it'll hold for maybe a week before it pulls out again. I ended up having to shim the hinges with some thin brass plate I had lying around just to get the gap even. Brass is great for that, it won't rust like steel when it's exposed to the weather. \n\nAnyway, it closes with a nice, satisfying click now. But yeah, perfectionism? Not really. I just like things to work the way they're supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Even though others, like your doctor, have told you that you're underweight, do you still feel that your body is too heavy or that certain parts of your body are too large?\n\nPatient: Didn't we just... I feel like you just asked me this a minute ago. But no, like I told you, I don't sit around feeling like my body is too heavy or that my stomach or whatever is too big. I really don't pay attention to it. \n\nHeavy, though... man, if you want to talk about heavy, you should have seen the load of lumber I had to pick up from the mill on Tuesday. I'm building this custom farmhouse dining table for a client, and they insisted on solid 8/4 quarter-sawn white oak for the top. Do you have any idea how dense that stuff is? It's like lifting solid concrete. It's got to be pushing forty-seven pounds per cubic foot. I had six of these massive eight-foot slabs in the bed of my truck, and I could actually hear the leaf springs groaning when I went over the speed bumps leaving the yard. \n\nI really need to upgrade the suspension on that truck if I'm going to keep taking these custom furniture jobs. Or at least invest in a proper heavy-duty utility trailer with a dual axle. The problem with trailers, though, is finding a place to store them. My driveway is barely wide enough as it is, and my neighbor, Dave—he's got this massive RV that he parks right on the property line. It's a total eyesore, one of those fiberglass monstrosities from the early two-thousands, and the clear coat is peeling right off the top. I've told him a hundred times he needs to at least put a tarp over it before the rain gets into the roof seams and delaminates the whole thing, but he never listens. Once water gets into that composite core, it's game over. You can't just patch it; you're looking at thousands of dollars in structural water damage. \n\nBut anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my weight. Yeah, no, I don't feel like I'm too large. I just don't see it that way.\n\nDoctor: Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel, in general, that your body is heavier than it actually is?\n\nPatient: No, I... I don't feel like that. I don't walk around feeling heavy at all. \n\nSpeaking of heavy, though, you want to know what really makes you feel heavy? A fully loaded leather tool belt. When I first started out, I bought this gorgeous Occidental Leather rig. Beautiful craftsmanship, heavy saddle leather, but my god... you put a 22-ounce Estwing hammer in the loop, a couple pounds of galvanized framing nails, a 35-foot tape measure, a speed square, chalk line... you're carrying an extra twenty pounds right on your hips all day. \n\nBy the time Friday rolled around, my lower back was always just completely shot. You really have to invest in a good set of padded suspenders to shift that load up to your shoulders. Though, honestly, even then, it just moves the pain from your lumbar spine right up to your trapezius muscles. It's an ergonomic nightmare. I finally gave up and switched to a ballistic nylon rig about five years ago. Best decision I ever made. \n\nThe nylon doesn't hold up quite as well to abrasion, of course. Like, if you brush up against a rough-cut masonry wall or catch it on a Simpson strong-tie—those metal joist hangers have edges like literal razor blades—it’ll fray pretty quick. I was actually just patching up a tear in my main nail pouch with some heavy-duty upholstery thread last night because I refuse to buy a new one yet. They want like a hundred and fifty bucks for a decent setup now, which is just highway robbery for something that isn't even real leather. \n\nBut... sorry, I'm rambling again, aren't I? You were asking if I feel heavy. No. I don't. I just don't feel that way.\n\nDoctor: Even though others have told you that you're underweight and may need to gain weight for your health, do you still believe that your current weight or body shape is exactly where it needs to be and that gaining weight would be a loss of control?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not about what they think, it's... I mean, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have, you know, the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays, I just start worrying right away. I worry that I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep. \n\nSpeaking of grip, you wouldn't believe how hard it is to maintain a decent grip strength when you're working with old, dried-out hickory tool handles. I was restoring this antique drawknife last weekend—beautiful piece of high-carbon steel, probably from the late eighteen-hundreds, back when they really knew how to forge a blade. The edge retention on those old tools is incredible. You can get them sharp enough to shave with if you spend enough time on a leather strop with some green honing compound. \n\nBut the handles! They were completely loose. The wood had shrunk over the last century, and the tangs were just rattling around inside. People think you can just soak them in linseed oil to swell the wood back up, but that's a myth. It just makes a sticky mess and doesn't fix the structural integrity. You actually have to pull the handles off, wrap the tangs in a layer of thin brass shim stock—there's that brass again, see, it's so useful—and then drive them back in with a wooden mallet. You have to use a wooden mallet, or a dead-blow hammer, because if you hit the end of the handle with a steel hammer, you'll split the hickory right down the grain. \n\nAnyway, I spent three hours just getting those handles seated properly. It takes a lot of control to get it right without ruining the antique wood. But yeah... what were you asking? Oh, gaining weight. Yeah, if I eat those heavy foods, I just feel like I'm losing control of everything.\n\nDoctor: Even though you don’t focus on specific body parts, do you feel that staying at your current weight is extremely important for how you see yourself or your ability to function in daily life?\n\nPatient: No, I don't... I wouldn't say that. It's not like I wake up and think about my weight as part of who I am or how I function. I don't really tie it to my identity like that. \n\nFunctioning, though... man, if you want to talk about things needing to function properly, you should have seen the locking casters on the scaffolding I had to rent last week. I was installing some heavy multi-piece crown molding in this house with fourteen-foot ceilings—beautiful Victorian place, original plaster walls, just incredible bones. But the Baker scaffold they gave me at the rental yard? The spring pins on the height adjustment were completely shot. You're supposed to have a solid lock every two inches, but the springs were so rusted from being left out in the rain that they kept sticking open. \n\nDo you know how dangerous that is? If one side of that platform drops while you're up there balancing a twelve-foot piece of primed pine and holding a pneumatic brad nailer, you are going right down to the hardwood. And of course, the client had just had the floors refinished. Brazilian cherry. Gorgeous wood, takes a stain beautifully, but it shows absolutely every single scratch. If I dropped my compressor or my nail gun on that floor, I'd be buying them a whole new room of flooring. I ended up having to spray penetrating oil into the pins and work them back and forth with a pair of channel locks for like forty-five minutes just to get them to seat right so the platform would actually function safely. You really can't trust rental equipment these days, they just don't maintain it.\n\nBut... I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Oh, right, my weight and functioning. Yeah, no, I don't really see my weight as being important to how I function. I just go to work and do my job.\n\nDoctor: Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel that your body is heavier than it actually is?\n\nPatient: Wait, didn't we just cover this? I feel like you just asked me about feeling heavy. And like I said before, no. I don't feel heavier than I am. I really don't. \n\nIf you want to talk about something that's heavier than it looks, though, try lugging around a sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself. Medium-density fiberboard. People think because it's engineered wood, it's gonna be light, but a standard four-by-eight sheet weighs almost a hundred pounds. It is just dead, dense weight. And it has no real structural integrity on the edges, so if you drop a corner while you're carrying it, it just mushrooms out and ruins the whole piece. \n\nI was building these custom built-in bookcases for a client last month—they wanted them painted, so MDF is actually great for that because it takes paint beautifully, no grain to show through. But getting those sheets out of the back of my truck and onto the table saw? My god. You absolutely have to use one of those Gorilla Gripper panel carriers that clamps onto the top edge, otherwise your arms just aren't long enough to get a good center of gravity. Plus, when you cut that stuff, the dust is like talcum powder. It gets into absolutely everything. Your clothes, your eyes, the motor of your router... I go through so many shop-vac filters when I'm working with MDF. You really have to wear a good half-mask respirator, not just those cheap paper dust masks from the hardware store, or you'll be coughing up brown gunk for a week. \n\nAnyway... sorry. You're probably getting tired of hearing about my job. But yeah, to answer your question again, no. I don't feel heavy. I just don't have that problem.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or worried about things in your daily life, even when there doesn’t seem to be a clear reason for it?\n\nPatient: Anxious? No, I wouldn't say I get anxious for no reason. I mean, if I'm worried about something, there's usually a pretty good reason for it. I'm a pretty practical person. \n\nSpeaking of practical, I was just thinking about how impractical most modern hardware is. You go to the big box store to buy hinges for a cabinet door, and everything is that cheap pot metal from overseas. It looks shiny in the package, but the minute you put any real torque on the screws, the heads just snap right off. Pop! And then you're stuck trying to extract a broken screw shaft out of a piece of expensive oak face frame without ruining the wood. \n\nI actually had to invest in a specialized set of hollow-core extractor bits just for that. They're like these tiny little hole saws that drill around the broken screw. But even then, you have to plug the hole with a hardwood dowel, wait for the glue to cure, cut it flush with a Japanese pull saw—those saws are amazing, by the way, they cut on the pull stroke so the blade can be incredibly thin, which means less kerf and a way cleaner cut. Anyway, you have to do all that just to drill a new pilot hole and try again. It's a massive waste of time. I finally just started ordering all my hardware from this specialty supplier out of Pennsylvania. It costs three times as much, but they use actual solid brass and hardened steel. When you're hanging a solid core door that weighs eighty pounds, you can't trust cheap hinges. You just can't. \n\nBut, uh, what were we talking about? Anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't just sit around worrying about nothing. If I'm worried, it's about something real, like a stripped screw or a deadline."
